items.text: The Life of a Famous Scientist

hints: Fiction is made-up story. Non-fiction gives facts.
Titles like How or A Guide to usually mean facts.
Ask: could this be a real event or a real topic?
items.explanation: Fiction tells invented stories. Non-fiction gives true information about real topics.

items.prompt: Which section of the library is best for a book called "A Visual Guide to the Planets"?

options.why: Poetry books are made up of poems.
This section holds stories with magic.
Playscripts hold plays to perform.

hints: Is the book made of facts or invented stories?
Non-fiction books are grouped by subject.
Look at the word Planets: what subject is it?
items.explanation: A guide to the planets gives facts, so it is non-fiction and is shelved with space and science books.

items.prompt: Match each genre to its main feature.
pairs: a puzzle and clues to solve
an invented story set in the past
hints: Think about the setting and the problem in each genre.
Match the clearest ones first.
Start with mystery: what does the reader try to do?
items.explanation: Each genre has typical features: science fiction looks to the future, mystery has clues, fantasy has magic and historical fiction is set in the past.

items.prompt: Which genre is this? "The old clock had stopped at midnight. Nobody had touched the locked drawer, yet the key now lay on the table. Putri counted the muddy footprints: five, leading to the window."

options.why: There is no magic or imaginary creature here.
There is no sign of space or future technology.
Nothing shows the story is set in the past.

hints: What problem does the character face?
Look for clues and an unexplained event.
Which genre is about solving a puzzle?
items.explanation: Locked drawers, muddy footprints and an unexplained key are clues, so this is a mystery.

items.prompt: Which genre is this? "In the year 2150 the ship Aster landed on a planet with two moons. Captain Leo asked the robot to scan the air before anyone left."

options.why: The setting uses technology, not magic.
There is no puzzle or clues yet.
The story is set on another planet, not on Earth.

hints: Look at the setting and the technology.
Spaceships and robots are clues to the genre.
Which genre imagines the future?
items.explanation: A starship, a robot and another planet make this science fiction.

items.prompt: Match each non-fiction text type to its purpose.
pairs: to tell someone how to do something
to give facts about a topic
to make the reader agree or act
hints: Think about what the writer wants the reader to do or learn.
Instructions tell you what to do step by step.
Start with persuasive text: what does it try to change?
items.explanation: Instructions guide, recounts retell, reports inform and persuasive texts try to change what the reader thinks.

items.prompt: Which text type is this? "First, wash the rice. Next, add two cups of water. Then bring it to the boil."

options.why: A recount tells what happened in the past.
A report gives facts and does not give orders.
An explanation says why or how something works.

hints: Look at the verbs at the start of each sentence.
Words like first, next and then show order.
Does the text tell you what to do?
items.explanation: Orders such as "wash" and "add" and the sequence words show that this is a set of instructions.

items.prompt: Which sentence is written in an impersonal style?

options.text: I think museums are amazing, and I visit one every month.
options.why: The words I and my make it personal.

options.text: Museums store and display objects of historical value.

options.why: The words you and our talk directly to the reader.

options.text: We had a great time at the museum.
options.why: The word we makes it personal.

hints: Personal style uses I, we or you.
Impersonal style states facts without talking about the writer.
Cross out sentences that use I, you or we.
items.explanation: The impersonal sentence states facts and does not use I, we or you.

items.text: I felt nervous before the race.
The race starts at nine o'clock.

hints: Look for words like I, we, our and you.
Impersonal style states facts as they are.
Ask: does the sentence talk about feelings or the writer?
items.explanation: Personal style uses I, we, our or you. Impersonal style states facts without those words.

items.text: a list of characters at the start

hints: Plays are written to be acted out.
Stories use narration and speech marks.
Think of what an actor needs to see on the page.
items.explanation: Playscripts have speaker names, stage directions and a cast list. Stories use narration and speech marks.

items.prompt: Which set of instructions is clearest for a reader?

options.text: Put the thing in the other thing and then do it up.
options.why: The words are vague, so the reader cannot follow them.

options.text: I like planting seeds in pots in my garden.
options.why: This tells a personal feeling, not steps.

options.text: 1. Place the seed in a small pot. 2. Cover it with soil. 3. Water it gently.
Seeds are interesting and many people grow them.
options.why: This is general information and gives no steps.

hints: Clear instructions use steps and exact words.
Look for numbers or sequence words.
Which option tells you exactly what to do?
items.explanation: Numbered steps with specific verbs and nouns make instructions easy to follow.

items.prompt: Choose all the features that suggest a text is a news report.

options.text: a diary-style opening such as Dear diary
options.why: A diary opening belongs to a personal recount.

options.text: quotations from people who saw the event

options.why: Ingredients belong to a recipe.

options.text: facts about who, what, where and when

hints: News reports tell what has just happened.
They answer who, what, where and when.
Which features would you see in a newspaper?
items.explanation: News reports have headlines, facts about the event and quotations from witnesses.

items.prompt: Story A: Tomo finds a lost wallet and returns it even though he needs money. Story B: Citra tells the truth about a broken vase even though she might be punished. What theme do both stories share?

options.why: Neither story has a battle.
The characters are not shown helping a friend.
Neither character is trying to find out something new.

hints: Ask what choice each character makes.
A theme is the big idea the story shares.
Both characters do the right thing when it is hard.
items.explanation: Both characters choose to do the honest thing even when it costs them, so the shared theme is honesty.

items.prompt: A leaflet says: "Don't miss out! Join our swimming club today and feel fantastic!" Which statement is true?

options.text: It is a report because it gives facts about swimming.
options.why: It has no facts, only strong claims.

options.text: It is a persuasive text because it uses exclamations and talks directly to the reader.
It is a recount because it tells what happened.
options.why: Nothing in it is about past events.

options.text: It is an explanation because it says how swimming works.
options.why: It does not explain how anything works.

hints: Think about the purpose of the leaflet.
Look at the punctuation and the way it addresses the reader.
Does it want the reader to do something?
items.explanation: The leaflet tries to make readers join the club, using exclamations and words such as "you" to persuade them.
